title: ECDIS familiarisation
plain: Have the Master and deck officers been familiarised with our ECDIS, and are the records on board?
why: An officer who cannot use the ship's own ECDIS properly can miss a grounding danger on watch.
checks: Company procedure for ECDIS familiarisation before taking a watch
Familiarisation checklists signed for the Master and each deck officer
Officer asked to demonstrate two items from the checklist
Whether anyone kept a watch before being familiarised
ready: Company ECDIS familiarisation procedure
Completed checklists for every deck officer, including the back-up unit
Type-specific training certificates, if your company process needs them
Nautical Institute checklist or equivalent company or maker checklist
traps: No procedure covering time scale, method, place, trainer, competency proof and records
Checklist missing or incomplete for an officer
Officer stood a watch before familiarisation was done
Officer cannot show checklist items on the ECDIS
Checklist much thinner than the Nautical Institute annex
Just watching another officer used as 'familiarisation'
say: Every deck officer completes a structured ECDIS familiarisation on our own units before taking a watch, as set out in our SMS. The checklist is signed off by an authorised trainer and kept on board. I can show you any item on the list on the ECDIS now.

practice.q: How were you familiarised with this ECDIS when you joined?
Show me how you would change the safety contour on this unit.
a: Value as set by company procedure and the passage plan
Check the change is applied on the screen

tip: Keep your own signed checklist copy handy and practise two or three items on the ECDIS before the inspector arrives.

title: ECDIS set up and operation
plain: Do officers know the company ECDIS procedures, and do records show ECDIS was used correctly through each voyage?
why: Wrong ECDIS settings or ignored alarms are a common cause of groundings.
checks: Company ECDIS procedure and checklists, including display and alarm settings
Safety contour and safety depth set for the ship's draught; safety frame set for speed and manoeuvring
Alarm history for alarms that proper set up should have avoided
Second ECDIS set up as the back-up in the same way
ready: ECDIS procedure, checklists and quick reference guides
Records of software updates done as the maker instructs
Records of periodic maker-required tests
Records showing settings checked regularly during each voyage
Defect entry for any faulty unit
traps: No procedure, or unclear on display, alarms, safety contours, safety frame or route checking
Officer cannot explain or operate the ECDIS fitted
Any ECDIS unit defective
Second ECDIS not set up as back-up
Settings wrongly entered at some point in the voyage
Passage plan does not mention needed ECDIS setting changes
say: Our SMS gives us checklists for setting up ECDIS, including display layers, safety contour and alarms. We check the settings regularly during the voyage and record it. If one unit fails, we use the back-up as per our contingency procedure.

practice.q: Which safety settings do you check before departure?
a: Safety contour and safety depth for draught
Alarm settings as in the passage plan

practice.q: What do you do if the main ECDIS fails?
What is CATZOC and what is SCAMIN?
a: CATZOC shows the accuracy of the chart depth data
Poor CATZOC areas need a bigger safety margin
SCAMIN is the smallest scale where a detail is shown

tip: Know where your alarm log is and be ready to explain any repeated alarm in it.

title: Radar and ARPA
plain: Do officers know how to operate and test the radar/ARPA, and do records show it was done?
why: Radar and ARPA are the main tools for spotting collision risk, so they must work and be used well.
checks: Company procedure for radar/ARPA use and performance checks
CPA and BCR alarm settings, with audible and visual alarms working
Parallel index set up compared with the passage plan
Heading, speed and position inputs match the master equipment
Magnetron change records
ready: Radar/ARPA procedure and quick reference guide
Records of operation and performance checks
Blind sector information for each radar
Magnetron change records against the planned interval
Parallel index data from the last passage
traps: No company procedure
Officer unaware of the danger of using AIS vectors for collision avoidance
Officer cannot explain X-band (9 GHz) and S-band (3 GHz) differences
Radar not in use or tested as the procedure requires
Wrong heading, speed or position feed
No blind sector indication, or magnetrons not changed on schedule
say: Our SMS says when radars are on, how we check them and what CPA and BCR alarms to set. I know X-band gives better detail and S-band copes better in rain and clutter. I do not rely on AIS vectors alone for collision avoidance.

practice.q: What is the difference between X-band and S-band radar?
a: X-band: better resolution, more affected by weather
S-band: better in rain and sea clutter

practice.q: Why not use AIS for collision avoidance on its own?
a: AIS data may be wrong or missing
Radar and visual look-out remain primary

tip: Know where the blind sectors are and show the marked diagram without being asked.

title: Steering control systems
plain: Do officers know how to operate, test and change over the steering systems, and are test records kept?
why: Loss of steering near land or traffic leaves very little time to react.
checks: Company procedure for modes, testing and changeover
Test records showing all modes tested from each location
Changeover instructions and block diagram posted on the bridge
Officer knows what to do when a steering alarm sounds
ready: Steering procedure and vessel-specific changeover steps
Emergency steering procedure
Block diagram for changeover of remote controls and power units
Steering test records from a recent voyage
traps: No company procedure
Officer unfamiliar with changing modes or reacting to steering alarms
Block diagram not permanently displayed on the bridge
Steering not tested or operated as the procedure says
Any steering control defect
say: We test steering before departure and arrival and during the voyage as our SMS requires, from every control position and mode. The changeover instructions and block diagram are posted here. If an alarm sounds, I follow the posted steps and call the Master.

practice.q: Take me through changing to the other steering system.
a: Use the bridge control or the steering room as procedure says
Inform the Master and engine room

practice.q: What do you test before departure?
a: All steering modes and control positions

tip: Practise explaining the changeover while standing next to the posted block diagram.

title: Automatic Identification System (AIS)
plain: Do officers know the company AIS procedure, and do records show regular AIS checks and tests?
why: Wrong AIS data misleads other ships, and an AIS left on in a gas area is an ignition risk.
checks: Company AIS procedure including switching on and off
Records of checks and performance tests
Heading, speed and position feeds match the master equipment
Static data entered correctly
Company guidance on AIS in collision avoidance
ready: AIS operation and testing procedure
Check and performance test records
Company guidance on use of AIS data for collision avoidance
Record of static data check
traps: No AIS procedure or no collision avoidance guidance
Officer unfamiliar with either
No records of checks and tests
AIS defective, wrong data feed or wrong static data
AIS left on alongside in a possible gas area without aerial isolation or dummy load, unless the shore asked for it
say: Our SMS covers AIS set up, data checks and tests. I check that static and voyage data are correct and the feeds match our master equipment. Alongside, AIS is switched off or the aerial isolated with a dummy load unless the terminal asks otherwise.

practice.q: What do you do with AIS alongside the terminal?
a: Gas risk: switch off or isolate aerial with dummy load

practice.q: How can AIS help with collision avoidance?

tip: Check your static data page before each port arrival and note it in the checklist.

title: Bridge watch alarm (BNWAS)
plain: Do officers know the BNWAS procedure, and do records show it was on and tested as required?
why: BNWAS calls for help if the officer on watch is incapacitated or asleep, so the bridge is never unwatched.
checks: Company BNWAS procedure: when on, who activates, who has the key or password
Bridge log and checklists showing BNWAS on and tested
Officer can explain or show activation and deactivation
Officer knows what to do at a stage 2 or 3 alarm
ready: BNWAS procedure
Bridge log book
Bridge checklists with BNWAS tests
Password or key arrangement limited to Master and authorised deputy
traps: No company BNWAS procedure
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure or the tests
BNWAS defective
Password or key known to people beyond the Master and authorised deputy
No records of operation or testing
Any modification to defeat the BNWAS
Procedure does not require BNWAS on at anchor (process negative)
say: Our SMS requires BNWAS on at sea and at anchor. Only the Master and his authorised deputy hold the password. We test it as the procedure says and record it, and I know the actions at each alarm stage.

practice.q: When must BNWAS be on?
a: Underway at sea, including when autopilot is used
Also at anchor per OCIMF expectation

practice.q: What happens if you do not reset it?
a: Visual indication then audible alarms in stages
Alarm reaches Master or other officers
Reset only from the bridge lookout area

tip: Check the BNWAS is switched on at anchor and logged, since many procedures miss that.

title: GNSS receivers
plain: Do officers know how the GNSS receivers are set up and checked, and was it done to company procedure?
why: Wrong GNSS position or datum feeds into ECDIS, AIS and radar and can mislead the whole bridge.
checks: Company GNSS procedure and receiver configuration
Antenna offset data entered correctly
WGS84 datum set
Periodic checks and test records
Position feed to two or more systems is correct
Posted instructions for any inter-switch arrangement
ready: GNSS management procedure
Records of periodic checks and tests
Antenna offset measurements
Posted switching instructions for the receivers
Procedure for single and multiple receiver failure
traps: No procedure for the receivers
Officer unfamiliar with procedure or equipment
Not configured per company needs, or antenna coordinates wrong
Periodic checks not done
Receiver defective
Wrong position going to AIS, ARPA or GMDSS equipment
say: Our SMS defines how the GNSS receivers are configured and checked. They are set to WGS84, and the antenna offsets are entered from the ship's measurements. I compare the receivers regularly and know what to do if one or all fail.

practice.q: What datum should the GNSS be set to?
What if one GNSS receiver fails?
a: Switch output to the other receiver
Inform the Master, use other fixing methods

tip: Keep the antenna offset sheet with the GNSS records so you can show it quickly.

title: Echo sounder
plain: Do officers know how to use and check the echo sounder, and do records show it was used as required?
why: The echo sounder is the check on under-keel clearance when charts or positions may be wrong.
checks: Company echo sounder procedure
Recorder in use on a recent passage as required
Depth alarm set as the procedure says
Accuracy check records against water of known depth
Officer shows the reading under the keel now
ready: Echo sounder procedure
Records of recorder use and any time or position marks
Records of accuracy comparison
Depth alarm criteria
Notes for forward and aft transducer set up where fitted
traps: No procedure for the echo sounder and recorder
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
Officer cannot calculate depth under keel or verify accuracy
Echo sounder not operated or tested as procedure and maker require
Reading not as expected at inspection
Echo sounder or recorder defective, or alarm not set per procedure
say: Our SMS says when the echo sounder and recorder must run and how to set the depth alarm. We compare it with a known depth periodically and record it. I can show the depth under the keel and how I worked it out.

practice.q: How do you work out the depth under the keel?
a: Allow for transducer position and draught

practice.q: When must the echo sounder be on?
a: Depth alarm set to a safe value

tip: Know the transducer offset and the ship's draught by heart, because the inspector may ask you to calculate on the spot.

title: Speed and distance measuring devices
plain: Do officers know how the speed log is tested and used, and are the periodic test records available?
why: Wrong speed input gives wrong ARPA, AIS and ECDIS information, hiding collision and grounding danger.
checks: Company procedure for operation and testing of logs
Speed shown at repeaters, ARPA and ECDIS matches the master log
Ground speed on ECDIS matches the dual axis log, where fitted
Periodic function and accuracy test records
Records that speed input to ARPA, AIS and ECDIS was verified
ready: Speed log procedure and maker instructions
Periodic accuracy and function test records
Records of speed input verification to ARPA, AIS and ECDIS
Knowledge of which speed input each system uses
traps: No company procedure
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
Periodic log tests not completed as required
Speed input checks to navigation equipment not done
Remote displays or ARPA, AIS, ECDIS speeds differ from the master log
Log defective in any way
say: Our SMS sets periodic checks of the speed log and of the speed going to ARPA, AIS and ECDIS. I compare displays against the master log and record the result. I know which speed input each system should use.

practice.q: Which speed input should the ARPA use?
How do you check the log is accurate?
a: Compare with GNSS and set or drift

tip: Check the speed input setting on every system at the same time, so any mismatch is found in one go.

title: Navigation lights and shapes
plain: Do officers know how navigation lights and shapes are tested, and is there proof they work and are visible correctly?
why: Wrong or failed lights and shapes mislead other ships about what you are and where you are heading.
checks: Company procedure for tests of lights, controller and shapes
Pre-departure, pre-arrival and daily checklists
Officer demonstrates the light controller and its alarms
Spare lamp inventory against each light fitted
LED lamp lifespan method
Shapes and portable lights sighted
ready: Navigation light test procedure and checklists
Spare lamp inventory with luminosity or wattage and where each fits
LED usage or lifespan records, if LED lamps are fitted
Three balls, one cylinder and one diamond in good condition
Portable lights with lanyards, where required
traps: No procedure for lights, controller and shapes
Lights or controller not tested as procedure says
Lights, screens damaged, moved or obscured so arcs or spacing are wrong
Shapes missing or unusable
Portable lights defective or not ready to rig
Spare lamps missing or wrong size, focal plane, luminosity or wattage
No guidance or method for LED lifespan, or LEDs used beyond their lifespan or in alarm
say: Our SMS has regular checks of the lights, the controller and its power failure alarm. Spare lamps match the maker's specification and are listed in the inventory. For LED lamps we track usage against the maker's lifespan. Shapes and portable lights are checked and ready.

practice.q: What does the navigation light controller check for you?
How do you know the LED lights are still bright enough?
a: Alarm for reduced intensity, or usage records

tip: Check the spare lamp list against the actual lamps in the store, not just on paper.

title: NAVTEX and SafetyNET
plain: Do officers manage NAVTEX and SafetyNET messages properly, and are warnings plotted on the voyage charts?
why: Missed navigational warnings can leave a ship heading into wrecks, lost cargo or restricted areas without knowing.
checks: Company procedure for handling maritime safety information
NAVTEX set for the right coast stations
SafetyNET receiver set for correct NAVAREA and coastal warning areas
Messages read, acknowledged, filed and plotted on charts
Expired warnings removed from charts
ready: MSI management procedure
Filed NAVTEX and SafetyNET messages
Current NAVAREA and coastal warnings on board
Charts, paper and electronic, showing plotted warnings
traps: No company procedure
Officer unfamiliar with procedure or equipment
NAVTEX or EGC receiver defective
NAVTEX not set to stations on the route
SafetyNET not set to the right areas
Messages not acknowledged and filed per procedure
say: Our SMS says NAVTEX and SafetyNET must be set for our route, and every message is read, acknowledged and filed. Warnings affecting us go onto the paper and electronic charts, and are removed when cancelled.

practice.q: How do you set NAVTEX for this voyage?
What do you do with a warning that affects our route?
a: Plot on paper and electronic charts
Tell the Master and update the plan
File the message, remove when cancelled

tip: Review NAVTEX settings at every change of coast station area and note it in the handover.

title: Preserving VDR data
plain: Do officers know how to save VDR data after an incident, and are the VDR tests on record?
why: If VDR data is overwritten, investigators lose the facts, and VDR faults are often only found after an accident.
checks: Company procedure for VDR set up, use, testing and data preservation
Save instructions posted near the VDR controls
Annual performance test by an approved facility
Test after repair or upgrade of the VDR or of equipment feeding it
Retention period declared in the pre-inspection questionnaire
ready: VDR procedure including when to preserve data
Emergency checklist that includes VDR data saving
Annual performance test report
Records of tests after maintenance or repair of the VDR or feeds
VDR specification showing how long data is kept
traps: No VDR procedure or no clear rule on preserving data
Officer unfamiliar with VDR management or data saving
VDR defective
Annual test not done by an authorised agent
No test after VDR repair, or after repair of equipment giving it data
Declared retention too short: minimum 12 hours if installed before 1 July 2014, 720 hours after
say: Our SMS tells us to save VDR data after any incident, not only navigation ones. The saving steps are posted at the VDR. The annual test was done by an approved service agent, and we test after any repair to the VDR or its data sources.

practice.q: Something has happened. What do you do about the VDR?
a: Save the data immediately as posted

practice.q: When must the VDR be tested?
a: After repair of equipment feeding it

tip: Be able to point to the save button and the posted instruction without searching.

title: Magnetic and gyro compasses
plain: Do officers know the company compass procedures, and do records show the compasses are accurate and reliable?
why: Wrong heading feeds into radar, ECDIS and AIS and can throw out the whole navigation picture.
checks: Company compass procedure
Magnetic, gyro and repeaters show consistent headings, illumination works
Compass error records for each compass
Deviation card and adjustment certificate
Gyro service records
ready: Compass management procedure
Compass adjustment and residual deviation certificate
Compass error log for each compass
Up-to-date deviation card on the bridge
Gyro service records
traps: No procedure for compasses
Officer unfamiliar with procedure or equipment
Compass error not recorded for each compass
Magnetic compass deviation regularly over company tolerance
Compass or repeater showing wrong heading
Manual speed or latitude correction set wrongly on gyro
Gyro service overdue by more than 5% of interval
say: We check compass errors each watch where possible and record them. The deviation card is on the bridge and the gyro is serviced to the maker's schedule. I know our company tolerance and when the magnetic compass needs adjustment.

practice.q: How often do you check compass error?
When should the magnetic compass be adjusted?
a: No error records for two years

tip: Check repeater headings against the master gyro every watch and after big manoeuvres, and log it.

title: VHF/DSC radios
plain: Do officers know how the VHF/DSC radios are used and tested, and are the checks recorded?
why: VHF is vital for distress and bridge communication, but misused for collision avoidance it causes confusion and errors.
checks: Company VHF/DSC procedure and Master's standing orders on VHF
Test records and the GMDSS radio log
Correct channels monitored at sea and in the passage plan
Static and dynamic data correct on the DSC units
Which VHF units are not connected to the VDR
ready: VHF/DSC use and testing procedure
GMDSS radio log book
Periodic test checklists
Master's standing orders
Marked list of VHF units not connected to the VDR and rules for their use
traps: No procedure for use and testing
Officer unfamiliar with procedure or equipment
Officer unaware of hazards of using VHF in collision avoidance
Tests not done, or critical communications not recorded
Wrong channels monitored
Wrong DSC position or MMSI data
Non-VDR VHF units not identified, with no limits on use for critical calls
say: Our SMS sets which channels we monitor, the tests and what we log. DSC data is checked as part of our routine tests. I do not use VHF to agree collision avoidance action, because it can cause confusion.

practice.q: Why not agree passing actions by VHF?
a: Risk of confusion and wrong identification

practice.q: Which VHF channels must you monitor?
a: Channel 16 and DSC channel 70 at sea
Others as the passage plan and company say

tip: Mark non-VDR handsets clearly so a critical call is never made on an unrecorded set.

title: Daylight signalling lamp
plain: Do officers know how to test and use the daylight signalling lamp?
why: It is the visual way to get another ship's attention by day or night if other means fail.
checks: Company procedure for use and testing
Test records in bridge equipment checks
Lamp tested on battery and on mains power
At least three spare bulbs of the right specification
ready: Procedure on attracting attention of another vessel and testing the lamp
Bridge equipment test records
Three or more correct spare bulbs
Charged battery
traps: No procedure for use and testing
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
Lamp defective, including battery operation
Fewer than three spare bulbs, or wrong type
say: Our SMS covers when we use the daylight signalling lamp and how we test it. I test it on both battery and mains power. At least three correct spare bulbs are kept on board.

practice.q: Show me that the lamp works on battery.
How many spare bulbs do you carry?

tip: Count the spare bulbs at every test and write the number in the record.

title: Sound signalling equipment
plain: Do officers know how to use and test whistle, bell and gong, and do records show sound signals were made in restricted visibility?
why: In fog, sound signals are the only way other ships know you are there.
checks: Company procedure for use of sound signals
Periodic test records for whistle, bell, gong and automation
Bridge log or restricted visibility checklist entries for sound signals
Last month's records for periods of restricted visibility
ready: Sound signalling procedure
Bridge equipment test records
Bridge log book
Completed restricted visibility checklists (BPG B13 or equivalent)
Evidence from the last three restricted visibility occasions
traps: No company procedure on sound signals in restricted visibility, collision avoidance and manoeuvring
Officer unfamiliar with the expectations
No test records for equipment and its automation
Equipment or automation defective
No record that signals were made in restricted visibility
say: Our SMS says what signals we sound in restricted visibility, when manoeuvring and at anchor. We test whistle, bell, gong and the automation regularly and record it. I can show you the log entries from our last fog periods.

practice.q: What do you do when visibility drops?
How do you test the sound signals?

tip: Write the start and stop time of fog signals in the log every time, because that is what the inspector will look for.

title: Passage planning
plain: Is every voyage planned berth to berth, checked, approved and followed, and can the officers explain the plan?
why: Most groundings and collisions start with a plan that was weak, not checked or not followed.
checks: Company passage planning and record keeping procedures
A recent plan in the company format, approved by the Master and signed
The same plan on ECDIS and paper charts with required information
Route checking done, and repeated after any change
Passage briefing with Master, navigation officers and an engineer
Position fixing at the planned method and interval
ready: Passage planning procedure
Appraisal form or checklist for a recent voyage
Signed passage plan
ECDIS or chart showing monitoring history
Bridge log, movement book and other voyage records
Plan on both ECDIS units where two are fitted
traps: No standard plan form or no appraisal checklist
Charted plan missing information the procedure requires
Plan not reviewed or approved as per procedure
Route check not done before sailing or after changes
Plan not followed, such as passing a mark on the wrong side
Manual position fixes not made as planned
Voyage records not kept
say: We plan every voyage berth to berth: appraise, plan, brief, execute and monitor. The Master approves after route checking and we brief with an engineer present. If conditions force a change, we re-check and re-approve the route before following it.

practice.q: Take me through how this passage was planned.
a: Plan berth to berth with no-go areas and fixing methods

practice.q: What do you do if you must leave the planned track?
a: Update, re-check and re-approve the plan

tip: Know where your contingency and abort positions are on the plan, since inspectors like to ask about them.

title: Under keel clearance (UKC) policy
plain: Do officers know the company UKC policy, and do records show UKC was calculated and kept as required?
why: Too little water under the keel means grounding, and many factors reduce it beyond the charted depth.
checks: Company UKC policy and minimum values for each phase
Calculation for a recent voyage with all required factors
Calculation done for the time of passing the critical area
UKC reviewed in the Master and pilot exchange
Squat information available on the bridge for loaded and ballast
Values in the pre-inspection questionnaire match the policy
ready: UKC policy and procedure
UKC calculations for recent voyages
Passage plan documents
Master and pilot exchange form with UKC data
Squat data for loaded and ballast
Echo sounder records and logs to prove passing times
traps: No UKC policy, or no required calculation points
Officer unfamiliar with how to calculate and record UKC
Required calculations not done
Policy broken without company permission
Calculation not made for the expected time of passing the critical point
Speed more than 10% above the calculated speed at the critical point
Error in the data or the calculation
Squat information not at hand on the bridge
say: Our SMS sets the minimum UKC for open sea, coastal, port, anchor and berth. We calculate with tide, density, squat, heel, wave response and chart reliability, for the time we actually pass the critical point. The numbers go into the Master and pilot exchange.

practice.q: What factors go into your UKC calculation?
What if the passage is delayed?
a: Recalculate for the new time over the critical area
Follow company action if UKC cannot be kept

practice.q: When can you go outside the company UKC policy?
a: Only with clear permission from the company
Ask the company before the passage
Keep the written answer with the passage plan

tip: Keep a worked UKC sheet for the current passage ready, and update the tide time if the ETA changes.

title: Master's standing orders and daily orders
plain: Has the Master written standing orders and daily orders covering key navigation rules, and have all navigation officers signed them?
why: Officers on watch need the Master's clear limits and call-me rules, written down, so they act early.
checks: Company procedure requiring standing and daily orders
Standing orders signed by the Master and by each navigation officer
Content: restricted visibility, CPA and BCR, passing distances, ECDIS alarms and layers, calling the Master, taking the con
Bridge order book entries at least daily, dated, timed and signed
Each officer signs daily orders before taking the watch
ready: Master's standing orders, signed and dated on joining or at update
Bridge order book with current daily entries
Signatures of all navigation officers on standing orders
Orders that refer to SMS procedures and do not weaken them
traps: Master has no own signed standing orders
Officers have not signed them (unless joined that day)
Orders weaker than the company SMS, in standing or daily orders
Missing items: restricted visibility, CPA/BCR, passing distance, ECDIS alarms and layers, calling the Master, taking the con, AIS and VHF limits
Daily orders not written, signed, dated and timed, or do not suit the voyage
OOW has not signed daily orders
Records show orders were not followed
say: The Master's standing orders support our SMS and are signed by every navigation officer when they join. Daily orders are written each day for the voyage conditions and I sign them before I take the watch. I know the CPA, passing distance and call-the-Master limits.

practice.q: When must you call the Master?
What are the minimum CPA and passing distances in the orders?
a: State the values in the standing orders
What to do if they cannot be kept

tip: Read the orders again at each watch handover, so you can quote the limits without opening the book.
refs: STCW Code Part A Ch VIII

title: Electronic chart management
plain: Are electronic charts (ENC and RNC) official, permitted, fully corrected and used correctly?
why: An out-of-date or unpermitted chart can hide a new danger and leave the ECDIS unfit for navigation.
checks: Company procedure for obtaining, permitting and correcting ENCs and RNCs
System that tracks which charts have valid permits
Charts for the last voyage were available and permitted on each ECDIS
Update history shows latest notices applied, including T and P notices
Officer shows how T and P notices are applied
Any RNC use only in RCDS mode with ENC not available and paper charts corrected
ready: Electronic chart management procedure
List of active permits or Pay As You Sail records
ENC status report, where available
Passage plan records showing the charts used
Update records to the latest notices to mariners
Plan for any gap in ENC coverage
traps: No procedure for ENCs and RNCs
Wrong declaration of primary means of navigation
Officer unfamiliar with correcting charts or applying T and P notices
No system tracking permits
Permits expired before or during a voyage
Voyage made with missing chart coverage
Charts not updated to latest notice
RNCs used when ENCs existed, or RCDS used without corrected paper charts
No system tracking corrections applied
say: Our SMS defines which charts we carry, how we track permits and how we apply updates and T and P notices. I can show the update history for any ENC. If ENC coverage is missing, we plan for it with fully corrected paper charts.

practice.q: How do you know the ENCs are up to date?
a: Check update history or ENC status report
T and P notices applied or overlay used

practice.q: When can RNC be used?
a: Only if no ENC is available

tip: Check permit expiry dates for the next voyage at the planning stage, not on sailing day.

title: Paper chart management
plain: Are paper charts official, corrected and kept in good condition, and do officers know the company procedure?
why: An uncorrected or worn paper chart can give wrong or hidden hazard information.
checks: Company paper chart procedure
Chart portfolio list with edition dates
At least two charts for a recent voyage spot checked for corrections
T and P notices and NAVTEX or NAVAREA warnings applied, and removed when cancelled
Largest scale charts for the passage on board and used
ready: Paper chart management procedure
Chart portfolio records and correction records
Passage plan record of charts used
Weekly and cumulative notices to mariners
Company-agreed plan if charts were missing for a port
traps: No paper chart procedure
Officer unfamiliar with the correction procedure
Voyage with missing or wrong scale charts, with no company mitigation
No systematic process to apply and remove T and P and warnings
Charts not corrected to the latest notice, or old editions used
Charts torn, stained or worn so detail is hidden
say: Our SMS covers identifying charts for the voyage, correcting them before planning, and tracking those not in use. Temporary notices and warnings are applied and removed when cancelled. I can show you the portfolio list and the corrections on any chart we used.

practice.q: How do you correct a chart?
a: Check it against the last one applied

practice.q: What if we are sent to a port and lack the charts?
a: Order charts as soon as possible

tip: Keep the correction log tidy and in date order, since that is the first thing an inspector opens.

title: Testing navigation equipment, engine, steering and thrusters
plain: Are navigation equipment, main engine, steering and thrusters tested before use and before critical phases, with checklists to prove it?
why: Finding a defect in steering or engine before arrival is far safer than finding it in restricted waters.
checks: Company procedure on testing at defined points
Vessel-specific checklists for steering test, preparation for sea and preparation for arrival
Completed checklists and bridge and engine logs from a recent voyage
Defects from tests entered into the defect system
Rudder timing checked hard-over to hard-over against earlier tests and maker's data
Flag waiver on board if steering tests are weekly on short voyages
ready: Testing procedure and vessel-specific checklists
Completed checklists for recent voyages
Bridge and engine log books
Defect reports for any problems found
Rudder timing records
Flag waiver, if used
traps: No procedure with defined test points
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure or with a checklist item
No evidence rudder hard-over timing was checked
Tests required by procedure not done
No flag waiver where tests were not within 12 hours before departure
Defect not entered in the defect system
Open defect at inspection (also hardware negative)
say: Our SMS defines tests before sailing, before arrival and before critical phases, using vessel-specific checklists. We test steering within 12 hours before departure and record rudder timing. Any defect goes straight into the defect system.

practice.q: What do you test before departure?
a: Steering, engine ahead and astern, alarms

practice.q: What do you do with a defect found during testing?
a: Tell the Master and engine room
Enter in the defect reporting system
Plan the repair and any mitigation

tip: Write the rudder hard-over times each test so you can compare them quickly if asked.

title: Nautical publications
plain: Are the required nautical publications on board, up to date, and managed to company procedure?
why: Old or missing publications give outdated information on lights, tides, routeing and port rules.
checks: Company procedure for managing, ordering and updating publications
List of mandatory and discretionary publications
Latest editions on board and corrected
Electronic publications accepted by flag, with back-up as on the Safety Equipment Certificate Form E
Hard copy of International Code of Signals and IAMSAR on board
ready: Publications procedure
Inventory with edition date and latest correction
Flag approval for electronic publications, where used
Back-up arrangement evidence
Printed International Code of Signals and IAMSAR
traps: No procedure for managing and updating publications
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
No inventory of mandatory and discretionary titles
Publications missing, obsolete or uncorrected
Electronic publications without flag approval or required back-up
say: Our SMS lists the mandatory and discretionary publications and how we update them. The inventory shows each edition and last correction. Electronic publications are flag-accepted with back-up, and the emergency books are in hard copy.

practice.q: Which publications must be in hard copy?
How do you know a publication is current?
a: Inventory with edition and correction date

tip: Check the inventory against the shelf regularly, and always before an inspection, and tick the list.

title: Minimum bridge team composition
plain: Do officers know the minimum bridge team and engine room mode for each stage of a voyage, and did recent voyages follow it?
why: A short-handed bridge or unprepared engine room in a risky area removes the safety margin.
checks: Company procedure for bridge team and engine room mode in all conditions
Plan shows expected bridge team and engine room mode changes
Logs show the plan was followed
Hand steering used when required, OOW not sole lookout against procedure
Changes in bridge team level and times are logged
ready: Bridge team composition procedure
Passage plans showing team and machinery status changes
Bridge log book, bell book and checklists
Bridge manning matrix with role of each team member
traps: No procedure for all stages including anchor, drifting, at-sea STS, DP work or underway transfers
No procedure on engine room status and manning
Officer unfamiliar with the procedures
Procedure unclear on hand steering
Plan lacks team composition or engine room mode, or has them wrong
Plan not followed at any stage
OOW as sole lookout against procedure
Changes in bridge team level and time not logged
say: Our SMS sets the minimum bridge team and engine room mode by hazards, traffic, weather and visibility. The passage plan shows when they change, and we log each change with the time. The OOW is not sole lookout unless the procedure allows it.

practice.q: What bridge team do you need now and when does it change?
a: As per passage plan and procedure
Higher level in traffic, poor visibility, near hazards
Log the time of every change

practice.q: When is hand steering required?

tip: Add team level changes to the passage plan sheet as waypoints, so the log matches the plan.

title: Machinery space team composition
plain: Do engineers know when the machinery space is attended or unattended and the team needed, and do records confirm it?
why: The bridge needs engine response at the right time, especially in confined waters, traffic or poor visibility.
checks: Company procedure for machinery space mode and team at each stage
Engine room log book and daily order book from a recent voyage
Planned status changes communicated to engineers at planning and daily
Roles of each team member when attended
Records of changes in status and team composition
ready: Machinery space status and manning procedure
Engine room log book
Engine room daily order book
Passage plan showing when to attend the machinery space
Records of status changes
traps: No procedure for attended or unattended mode, including anchor, drifting, STS, DP or underway transfers
No procedure for team composition
Engineer unfamiliar with the procedure
Required status not communicated to engineers
Records show the plan was not followed
Team not as the procedure requires when attended
No records of status or team
say: Our SMS sets when the engine room must be attended and with which team, based on hazards, traffic and visibility. The Chief Engineer and Master agree this at planning, and it goes in the daily order book. I can show the log entries for recent status changes.

practice.q: When does the engine room go from unattended to attended?
a: As per passage plan and company procedure
Before restricted waters, traffic or low visibility

practice.q: How do you know the plan ahead?

tip: Write the expected status change times in the daily order book each day, so night engineers know.
refs: ICS Engine Room Procedures Guide 1st ed

title: Integrating the pilot into the bridge team
plain: Is the pilot (or similar role) brought into the bridge team by a documented Master and pilot exchange?
why: Many accidents happen when the pilot and the bridge team do not share the same plan.
checks: Company procedure for integrating a pilot or similar role
Master and pilot exchange and pilot card from two recent operations
Time of exchange completion and time of transfer of the conn recorded
Defects noted on the pilot card
Officer understands every item on the checklists
ready: Pilot integration procedure
Completed master and pilot exchange and pilot card forms
Bridge log and bell book with conn handover times
List of equipment defects to tell the pilot
traps: No procedure or no checklists
Officer not familiar with the procedure or the checklist items
Forms missing for operations with a pilot
Forms incomplete or with wrong safety information
Time of exchange completion not recorded
Conn transfer times not recorded
Defects affecting navigation or mooring not shown on the pilot card
say: Before the pilot takes the conn, we complete the exchange: ship particulars, plan, ECDIS settings, UKC, tugs, mooring and any defects. We record when the exchange is complete and when the conn changes hands. It is repeated for a change of pilot.

practice.q: What do you tell the pilot on boarding?
a: Pilot card and ship manoeuvring data
Passage plan, UKC and ECDIS status

practice.q: What if the pilot refuses to sign?
a: Record the time of completed exchange

tip: Have the pilot card and defect list ready on the bridge before the pilot boards, so the exchange happens before the conn moves.

title: Bridge distractions
plain: Do officers know the company rules to prevent distraction on the bridge, and are they followed?
why: Distracted watchkeepers miss targets and hazards.
checks: Company procedure on bridge access, phones and devices, communications, non-essential activity, internet and email
Any sign on the bridge of the rules being broken
Officer explains the rules
Management of cargo or machinery monitoring if the bridge is multi-function
ready: Bridge distraction procedure
Posted bridge access and device rules
Internet and email rule for the bridge
If a combined bridge: how cargo and machinery monitoring is managed without distracting the team
traps: No procedure, or a gap in any area: access, devices, communications, non-essential activity, internet and email, combined bridge
Officer unfamiliar with the rules
Rules visibly not followed (phones, visitors, non-essential tasks)
say: Our SMS limits bridge access to those with a bridge duty, controls phones and personal devices, and keeps calls and internet use to safe navigation needs. We keep the bridge free from non-essential tasks.

practice.q: Who may come onto the bridge?
Can you use your phone on watch?
a: Only if the Master approves the situation
Internet and email for navigation needs only

tip: Put the access and phone rules where visitors see them at the bridge door.

title: EPIRB
plain: Do officers know how to operate and test the EPIRB, and is it in good order with inspection records?
why: The EPIRB is the ship's automatic distress alert. If it does not float free and transmit, rescue is delayed.
checks: Company procedure for inspection, testing and maintenance
EPIRB armed, able to float free, clear of obstruction, undamaged
Battery and hydrostatic release expiry dates
Lanyard fitted, neatly stowed, not tied to the ship or bracket
Instructions and manual present at the beacon
Officer explains self-test, manual operation and what to do after an accidental activation
ready: EPIRB procedure
GMDSS radio log book with inspections and self-tests
Annual test record
Five-yearly shore-based maintenance record (or sooner if flag requires)
Pictorial operating instructions at the beacon and the manual
traps: Officer cannot explain self-test, accidental activation or manual operation
EPIRB not armed, or not able to float free
Missing markings, instructions or manual
Casing damage, cracks or water ingress
Battery or hydrostatic release past expiry
Lanyard tied to the ship or bracket, or in poor condition
Incomplete records of inspections, self-tests, annual test or shore maintenance
EPIRB defective
say: We inspect the EPIRB and self-test it as the maker says, and record it in the GMDSS log. Battery and release dates are in date, and annual and five-year servicing are on record. If it is activated by mistake, I stop it and contact the rescue centre straight away.

practice.q: What do you do if the EPIRB is activated by accident?
a: Call the local rescue coordination centre

practice.q: How do you self-test it?
a: Use the self-test switch only as maker says
Do not hold it long, to save battery

tip: Check the lanyard during your routine rounds, since it is the item most often found tied to the bracket.

title: Search and rescue transmitters (SARTs)
plain: Do officers know how to use and test SARTs, and are the SARTs in good order with records?

checks: Company procedure for inspection and testing
Self-test shown for each type of SART carried
SART stowed where it can be placed quickly in a survival craft, and marked with symbols
Operating and testing instructions and battery expiry marked on each unit
Officer explains how a SART shows on a radar screen and how to mount it
Lanyard present
ready: SART procedure
GMDSS radio log book
Inspection and self-test records
Stowage position with correct symbol
Battery expiry dates clear on each SART
traps: No company procedure
Officer unfamiliar with purpose or operation
Officer cannot show how to mount it in a lifeboat or raft
Officer cannot describe radar display or explain self-test
Stowage place not marked with symbols
Operating instructions or battery expiry not marked
Battery out of date or lanyard missing
SART not where required or defective
Incomplete inspection and test records
say: Our SMS sets regular inspection and self-test of each SART. I can show how to mount one in a survival craft, and what it looks like on a radar: a line of dots. Batteries are in date and stowage is marked.

practice.q: What would a SART look like on a rescue ship's radar?
a: Shows the position of the craft in distress
AIS-SART shows on AIS display instead

practice.q: How often do you self-test it?
a: As company procedure and maker say
Short test only, to save battery

tip: Practise the self-test on each type of SART you carry, since they work differently.

title: Survival craft portable VHF radios

Records of inspection and tests
Enough radios on board, stowage marked with symbol and number
Colour or yellow/orange marking, operating instructions and battery expiry on the radio
Seal on primary battery intact, strap with weak link, clothing attachment
Controls so radios used on board are not taken into gas hazardous areas

GMDSS radio log book
Inspection and test records
Spare primary batteries, sealed and in date
Marked stowage location
traps: No procedure, or no guidance on non-emergency use
Officer unfamiliar with purpose, operation or testing
Too few radios
Stowage not marked with symbol and number
Radio or battery not yellow/orange or marked
Missing operating instructions
Battery past expiry or seal broken
Other batteries not clearly different from distress batteries
No clothing attachment or strap with weak link
Incomplete records or defective radios
say: The survival craft radios are tested to our SMS and logged. Distress batteries are sealed and in date. If we use them for shipboard work, our procedure keeps them out of gas hazardous areas.

practice.q: Where are the survival craft VHF radios kept?
a: Marked stowage with symbol and number
Ready to go to the craft
Number as required for the ship

practice.q: Can you use these for daily work?
a: Yes, if procedure allows and frequencies suit
Not in gas hazardous areas unless intrinsically safe
Keep sealed distress battery for emergencies

tip: Count radios and check seals at the same time as the monthly LSA inspection.

title: Distress, urgency and safety messages
plain: Do officers know how to send and receive distress, urgency and safety messages, with instructions posted at the GMDSS station?

checks: Company procedure for emergency communications with responsibility assigned

Instructions for sending distress and urgency messages posted at the equipment
IAMSAR Vol III, latest edition, at the GMDSS station
GMDSS log entries for received distress, urgency and safety messages
Officer explains how to send an alert and record messages

Station bill naming the GMDSS operator
Posted instructions at the radio station
IAMSAR Vol III
GMDSS radio log book

No qualified GMDSS operator named in the station bill
Instructions not displayed at the equipment
No IAMSAR Vol III at the station
Officer unfamiliar with procedure, watchkeeping requirements, how to send, or how to log messages
say: Our station bill names the GMDSS operator for a distress, and instructions are posted at the radio station. I know how to send a DSC distress alert and follow with a voice message, and I log all messages received. IAMSAR Vol III is at the console.

practice.q: How would you send a distress alert?
a: Use DSC or other GMDSS equipment
Follow with a voice message on the associated frequency, such as VHF channel 16 or 2182 kHz
Take care to avoid false alerts

practice.q: What do you do with a message you receive?
a: Record it in the GMDSS log
Act as per procedure and IAMSAR

tip: Make sure the posted instructions are readable and match the equipment actually fitted.

title: GMDSS station operation and testing

checks: Company procedure for operation, testing, maintenance and log keeping
Officer explains daily, weekly and monthly tests
GMDSS radio log, Form R or C record of equipment
Reserve battery locker, charging, and capacity test within 12 months
Shore-based maintenance agreement or other maintenance method
Aerials, GMDSS printer, radio station emergency lighting
ready: GMDSS procedure
GMDSS radio log book
Record of Equipment (Form R or C)
Reserve battery capacity test record
Shore-based maintenance records, in date
Printer paper in stock
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with operation

No battery capacity test in last 12 months

Log does not record all radio events
No shore-based maintenance evidence, or certificate expired
Equipment, printer, aerials or radio station lighting defective
say: We do GMDSS tests daily, weekly and monthly as per our SMS and log them. The reserve batteries are tested for capacity yearly. Our maintenance method is on record, and the log shows daily positions and any difficulties.

practice.q: What are the daily GMDSS tests?
What is on a monthly test?

tip: Check the battery locker PPE and ventilation at the monthly test, not just the batteries.

title: Radio and mobile phone use during cargo and ballast
plain: Does everyone know the danger of radios and mobile phones during cargo and ballast work, and are there enough intrinsically safe radios?

checks: Company procedure for radio and phone use in cargo and ballast work
No MF/HF transmissions, main antennae earthed or isolated
Fixed VHF/UHF on low power (one watt or less), portable radios one watt or less
Enough intrinsically safe portable radios in good order for cargo, ballast and bunkers
Phone restrictions shown at the gangway; non-intrinsically safe phones not outside accommodation
Any radio or radar repair raised at the pre-transfer conference
ready: Radio and phone procedure
Inventory of intrinsically safe VHF/UHF radios
Certificates for any intrinsically safe phones used outside accommodation
Phone rule notice at the gangway
Damaged radios withdrawn and marked
traps: No procedure, or Master, officer or rating unfamiliar with it
Too few intrinsically safe radios in working order
MF/HF repair or service not discussed at the pre-transfer conference
MF/HF transmissions during cargo or ballast
Main antennae not earthed or isolated
Fixed VHF/UHF not on low power
Portable radio over one watt, or a damaged radio used
Phone rules not shown at the gangway
Ordinary phone used outside accommodation, or intrinsically safe phone not marked or certified
say: At the berth we make no MF/HF transmissions and the antennae are earthed or isolated. Fixed VHF is on low power and our portable radios are intrinsically safe at one watt or less. Ordinary mobile phones stay inside the accommodation.

practice.q: Why are MF/HF transmissions banned alongside?
a: Radiated energy can induce a spark
Unearthed rigging or insulator arcing risk

practice.q: Where can phones be used?
a: Non-intrinsically safe phones only in accommodation
Intrinsically safe phones only if marked and certified

tip: Check the radio count and condition at each pre-arrival check, not only at the pre-transfer conference.

title: Annual DP trial report and drills
plain: Is the latest annual DP trial report on board, do officers know it, and have they done DP scenario drills?

checks: Company procedure for annual DP trials
Latest and previous trial reports on board
Trial within three months either side of the anniversary of the first FMEA proving trial
Report has findings list, close-out actions and a fitness statement for the DP class
Records of onboard DP training and drills
Officer explains the trial procedure and report contents
ready: Latest and earlier annual DP trial reports
Findings list with close-out records
Evidence of independent, competent witness
PMS test sheets, signed, if testing is a rolling programme
Records of DP scenario drills and training
traps: No procedure on annual DP trials
Latest or earlier reports not on board
Trial outside the three-month window, or date not reset after a new FMEA proving trial
No evidence of a competent independent witness
Rolling programme with no independent scrutiny, or incomplete and unsigned test sheets
Category A findings not shown as fixed, or findings open with no close-out or not in the SMS
No fitness statement or no findings list in the report
No evidence of DP drills
Officer unfamiliar with procedure or report
say: Our SMS sets the annual DP trial within three months of the anniversary date, with an independent witness. The latest report with its findings and close-outs is on board. We use the findings in our DP scenario drills, and records are kept.

practice.q: When must the annual DP trial be done?
a: Within three months before or after the anniversary
Reset after a new FMEA proving trial
Also after changes to the DP system

practice.q: What is in the report that matters to you?
a: Statement the vessel is fit for its DP class

tip: Review the open findings from the last report before the inspection so you can say how each was closed.

title: DP position reference systems

checks: Company procedures for PRS use at each offtake location
At least three different working PRS available to the DPO on offtake
Two independent differential satellite systems
PRS controls within easy reach of the DP control station
Sensor offset file with common reference point and sign convention
DP logbook and data log for PRS faults
ready: PRS procedures or field operator procedures
Sensor offset data file, updated after any sensor move
DP logbook
DP data log
Records of system or sensor changes with dates
traps: No procedures for PRS use at each offtake location
Officer unfamiliar with them
A PRS not in satisfactory condition
Fewer than three different working PRS on DP2 or DP3 during an offtake
Fewer than two independent differential satellite systems
PRS controls out of reach of the DP station
Offsets not filed or not readily available to DPOs
say: Our procedures and the field manual set which PRS we use at each location, and we keep at least three different working systems on offtake. The offset file is at the DP desk, measured from the common reference point, and updated when a sensor is moved.

practice.q: How many position references do you need on offtake?
a: Not all based on the same principle

practice.q: Where are the sensor offsets?
a: Filed and at the DP control station

tip: Mark the common reference point and sign convention on the offset sheet so any DPO reads it the same way.

title: DP events and incidents

Records of events and the DP fault log kept on board

System to share lessons from events
Investigations closed out in reasonable time

DP incident and event reports with close-outs
DP fault log
Independent data logger records for a minimum of one year
Evidence of experience transfer
traps: No procedure for recording, reporting and investigating
Events not reported by ISM or IMCA M 103 method
Reports not kept on board
Investigation not closed in reasonable time
DP fault records not kept on board
Logger data kept less than one year

Logger defective
No system to share lessons
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
say: We record DP incidents, undesired events and observations, and report them through our SMS or IMCA M 103. Reports and the fault log stay on board. Logger data is kept for at least a year, and lessons are shared across the fleet.

Different from an incident, which is total loss of DP

practice.q: What do you do after an event?

Completed DP checklists
Hard copy capability plots
DP footprint records
DP risk assessments, reviewed after changes
Consequence analysis software on DP2 or DP3

Not in a language DP operators understand
Manual missing checklists, instructions, risk assessment reviews or guidance on plots, footprints, consequence analysis and ASOG

say: The vessel-specific DP manual and hard copy capability plots are at the DP station. We complete the location and watchkeeping checklists and review risk assessments when locations or sensors change. Our ASOG sets generator numbers and power policy for each activity.

Alarm if thrust would be insufficient

Used as a decision support tool

title: Field operations manuals

Manual on board for each terminal the vessel trades to

Officer explains how to check the manual is the latest edition
Records of regular communication checks required by FSOG at the last terminal
